description: Machine-readable open-decision register. A question is RESOLVED only when an existing declaration already answers it; otherwise it is recorded with the arbiter it needs, the evidence gathered, the current interpretation and what is blocked until it is decided. Every row carries owner, affected domains, current interpretation, decision required, blocking level, date and references, so a future agent can continue without the historical chat. Nothing here is a silent choice.

decisions.question: Are the `lego.*` error codes named by the backend degradation vocabulary published?

Each carries `retryable` and a `retryRationale`. The registry rule that a code's namespace must equal a domain's declared `errorNamespace` is satisfied: domain `lego-foundation` declares `errorNamespace: "lego"`. All four codes named in the original finding (lego.capability_unavailable, lego.version_incompatible, lego.dependency_disabled, lego.migration_required) are published, so the degradation actions in interaction.mjs no longer name a code a consumer cannot look up.

decisions.question: Who owns the AI vocabulary - the frontend or the AI Foundation LEGO?
decisions.resolution: The manager owns it, as of P2.10: contract `ai.foundation@1.0.0` (domain `ai-foundation`, owner `manager`, status `contract-only`) declares the taxonomy, five provider kinds, eleven `ai.*` capability contracts, the 26 agent-event types, the trace/delegation/approval/artifact/context fields and the transport ladder. decisions.question: Which permission namespace do AI capabilities use?
decisions.finding: Two namespaces exist for the same grants. The published AI operations require 22 `ai:*` names (`ai:model:invoke`, `ai:agent:invoke`, `ai:agent:delegate`, `ai:app:read`, ...), while the six frontend AI capabilities declare `inference:invoke`, `agent:run`, `agent:observe`, `agent:delegate`, `workflow:write` and `execution:escalate`. Four of the six are the same grant as a published `ai:*` name; `workflow:write` and `execution:escalate` name grants whose domains publish no permission names at all.

decisions.frontendBehaviour: Nothing is renamed silently. The lock declares the mapping (`inference:invoke -> ai:model:invoke`, `agent:run -> ai:agent:invoke`, `agent:observe -> ai:agent:read`, `agent:delegate -> ai:agent:delegate`), each unmapped word carries the reason it exists, and the frontend refuses an undeclared permission word instead of accepting it as a synonym.

decisions.question: Which Skill operation set and contract version are canonical, now that an implementation exists?
decisions.resolution: Resolved by adopting the actual tested P2.12 shape rather than the larger proposed one. Canonical contract is ai.skill@1.0.0, owner manager, on the existing ai-foundation domain, now locked in apps/n8n-lego/src/lego/contracts/contract-lock.json. Canonical published operations are exactly four: skill.list, skill.resolve, skill.describe, skill.validate-selection. skill.register, skill.select, skill.load and skill.release were NOT published: they are internal lifecycle methods of the registry object. Publishing load would make lazy discovery a caller concern and defeat it; publishing register would let any caller mutate the vocabulary other consumers negotiate against. There is no execute operation and no ai:skill:execute permission, because execution is not a skill operation and no published name may imply that it is. The drift this row records — documents describing a Skill surface that did not match the code — is closed by locking the implemented shape so consumers have one published vocabulary.

decisions.question: Which contract rows and which rollover/continuation vocabulary does the manager publish for Context & Session, so the frontend binds to a lock row instead of to a version claim?
decisions.finding: Context & Session is one LEGO with two declared contracts and NO publication of its own. `manifest/ai-foundation.json` declares both shapes (`context`: 7 scopes, 9 fields, selective-load and compaction rules; `agentSession`: 10 fields, 3 references, 7 states, the bounded-size rule) and `manifest/domains.json` registers both as `contract-only` capabilities of the `ai-foundation` domain with 5 published operations in total (`ai.context.load`, `ai.context.compact`, `ai.agent-session.create`, `ai.agent-session.status`, `ai.agent-session.close`) and 5 permission words. `manifest/ai-lego-set.json#lego[id=context-session]` CLAIMS `ai.context@1.0.0, ai.agent-session@1.0.0` in its `versioning` string — but `contracts/contract-lock.json` publishes no row for either contract (15 rows at e754c5df: 10 lego.*/kernel/reference/auth rows, ai.foundation@1.0.0 and ai.skill@1.0.0). And nothing anywhere in the backend tree publishes the three vocabularies P2.13 is defined by: the rollover phases (NORMAL -> PREPARE -> ROLLOVER), the continuation package sections, and the continuity verification results (verified / degraded / failed). Those exist today only as the manager's P2.13 architecture ruling and as frontend planning prose (`.ai/master/CONTEXT_SESSION_MEMORY_PLAN.md`), which is exactly the shape XA-19 was raised for on the Skill side: a specification and an implementation with no published vocabulary between them. P2.13 UPDATE (2026-09-22, after agent-2 pushed its branch): agent-2 published both rows on `arena/01a0c6b5-n8n-rust-v-4` @ `fb254f32` — `ai.context@1.0.0` and `ai.agent-session@1.0.0`, owner `manager`, domain `ai-foundation`, status `implemented`, 17 locked rows in total — plus the contract surface module `apps/n8n-lego/src/lego/context-session.mjs` (`CONTEXT_SCOPES`, `CONTEXT_OPERATIONS` = load/compact/rollover/rehydrate/verify, `CONTEXT_MANAGER_STATES` = NORMAL/PREPARE/ROLLOVER, `CONTINUATION_FIELDS`, `CONTINUATION_VERIFICATION` = verified/degraded/failed, `AGENT_SESSION_STATES`, `AGENT_SESSION_OPERATIONS`, `AGENT_SESSION_TRANSITIONS`) re-exported by `context.mjs` and `agent-session.mjs`, and it moved `domains.json` to five `implemented` context operations. The frontend consumed that publication in the same cycle: the quoted set `contextOperation` went from 2 to 5 values, `continuationSection` was re-pointed from the AI-set manifest at the published `CONTINUATION_FIELDS`, `contextRolloverPhase` and `continuationVerification` were PROMOTED out of `PENDING_PUBLICATIONS` into quoted sets (values identical to the ruling), and `aiLegoStatus` adopted the sixth maturity word `in-progress` that agent-2 added to `statusVocabulary`. Two differences remain and are the manager's to rule: (1) `continuationSection` — the published contract spells two of the fourteen sections `toolStateReferences` and `importantReferences` while `ai-lego-set.json#lego[id=context-session].continuationPackage` still spells them `toolState` and `refs`, so one backend file contradicts the other; the frontend quotes the published contract and records the manifest spelling verbatim. (2) `contextOperation` — protected main still registers two operations `contract-only` while the peer branch registers five `implemented`; until the merge, a frontend lock that quotes five and a main tree that declares two are both truthful, which is why `test/29` and `test/32` bound the comparison to a tree that carries the publication and report the exact difference against one that does not.

decisions.frontendBehaviour: Against protected main @ e754c5df the surface reports `declared-not-locked` with `version: null`, renders no version, and answers every context/session affordance from the declaration it is handed. Against the publication agent-2 pushed at fb254f32 the same code reports `published` at 1.0.0 with no edit, because publication state is derived from the lock rows handed over. The frontend lock now quotes that publication: `contextOperation` = 5 (load, compact, rollover, rehydrate, verify), `continuationSection` re-pointed at the published `CONTINUATION_FIELDS` (so `toolStateReferences`/`importantReferences` are the rendered spellings), `contextRolloverPhase` and `continuationVerification` PROMOTED out of PENDING_PUBLICATIONS into quoted sets of `ai.context@1.0.0` with values identical to the ruling, and `aiLegoStatus` = 6 words including `in-progress`. Still refused: a fabricated token figure, a Memory store, an execution affordance, a transcript, chain-of-thought, a secret, a threshold at 100%, a silent reset, and any operation the UI would have to invent — `continue` is published by nobody, so `Continue session` stays `operation-unpublished` in both trees while naming the published path (ai.context.rollover -> rehydrate -> verify) it does not trigger. The two remaining differences (manifest section spelling; main's two-operation registry) are reported as data by declarationDrift, bounded by tests that only compare against a tree carrying the publication, and are NOT adopted silently.

decisions.frontendBehaviour: agent-1 does NOT edit the pin: it lives in the application's evidence script, it is a gate, and editing a gate to make a run green is what the merge protocol forbids. The check is reported FAIL with its measurement in the P2.13 evidence, the Context & Session view is built on demand so the boot path does not materialise a surface nobody has rendered, the surface prose is kept (a refusal that cannot explain itself is not a refusal a reader can act on), and the failure is recorded as B-14 in .ai/master/frontend/KNOWN_BLOCKERS.md and in the P2.13 knownLimitations. No other check regressed: 52/56 with three environmental failures and this one.

decisions.arbiter: manager: (A) raise the pin in apps/n8n-lego/scripts/capture-frontend-evidence.mjs to a stated budget with the measurement that justifies it (the pin was set at P2.8-F for a package that has since gained two AI surfaces); (B) rule that feature surfaces are opt-in imports rather than eager assembly, which changes how every later surface (Memory, Workspace, Token & Usage) is wired and needs a contract note, not just a code change; (C) rule that surface prose - refusal reasons, affordance details, lifecycle explanations - lives in manifest/*.json and is parsed on demand, which keeps the pin and moves ~100 KB off the import path without deleting anything; or (D) accept the red check for P2.13 and record it. agent-1 recommends (C) then (A): (C) is the design the Skill manifest already follows, and (A) is unavoidable by P2.14 whichever way (C) lands.
decisions.blocks: P2.13 evidence completeness (one check of 56 in the frontend boundary capture) and, at phase level, every later surface milestone: P2.14 (Memory) adds a third AI surface to the same eager import path, and the pin has no room for it. It does not block the P2.13 deliverables themselves - the vocabulary lock, the Context & Session surface, the milestone register and all 363 frontend tests pass, and `npm run lego:gate` does not include the evidence capture.
decisions.currentInterpretation: The pin measures the whole LEGO package at import, so it is a budget on the sum of every surface the frontend declares - not on the descriptor, which is unchanged at 18,126 B and is what the browser actually receives. Read that way the check is doing its job: it says the package has grown to the point where the next surface needs a decision about lazy loading, prose placement or the budget itself.
decisions.decisionRequired: manager: pick (A) raise the pin with a stated number, (B) make surfaces opt-in imports, (C) move surface prose into the manifests and parse on demand, or (D) accept the red check - and state which applies to P2.14.

decisions.relatedOpenDecision: None of the vocabulary rows: XA-20 is a publication question and this is a resource-budget question. It intersects B-10 (no installed dependencies in this sandbox), which is why three other checks in the same capture fail for environmental reasons and are reported as such rather than as regressions.

rules: A resolved row cites an existing declaration; an open row names its arbiter and what is blocked.
The frontend never picks a new shared word to end an open question — it fails closed and records the question.
A finding stays in the record after it is fixed, so the reasoning survives the fix.
The record is checked by tests: the lock is compared against the backend modules when they are present (test/29), and every open row states what the frontend does meanwhile.

A vocabulary quoted from a file with no publishing contract carries a structured `publicationPending` record naming the owner, the domain and a recorded decision - a free-text note is not enough, and an invented contract row is worse.
Every row names its owner, its affected domains, its current interpretation, the decision it requires, its blocking level and its references - a row without those is incomplete.
A superseded row is kept with a pointer to what replaced it; deleting history is not allowed.

alignment.how: The lock quotes values with provenance (contract id, version, owner, file, declaration). The test reads that declaration and compares the values, and it also compares the quoted *semantics* (the degradation actions and the callable lifecycle states). It skips with a stated reason only when the backend foundation is not on this branch at all; pointing `N8N_BACKEND_LEGO_ROOT` at a fetched backend tree runs it for real, and then a missing file is a failure, never a skip. The comparison itself is exercised (a renamed, a missing and an invented term must all be reported), so a pass means the check ran.
alignment.whenItRunsFully: after the backend foundation (apps/n8n-lego/src/lego/**, Agent 2) is on this branch

numbering.resolution: Neither series is renumbered: this register keeps XA-11 = the skill publication question, and agent-2's file keeps its proposal ids. Every frontend citation of XA-11 here means the skill question; a citation of XA-11 inside ai-lego-set.json means agent-2's AI-LEGO ownership proposal.
numbering.rule: A decision id is only half an address: the register it lives in is the other half. An id that collides across registers is recorded here rather than silently renumbered.
